{{Short description|Natural number between 89 and 91}}
'''90''' ('''ninety''') is the [[natural number]] following [[89 (number)|89]] and preceding [[91 (number)|91]].

{{Wiktionary|ninety}}
{{Infobox number
| number = 90
| divisor = 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 15, 18, 30, 45, 90 (12)
|lang1=[[Armenian numerals|Armenian]]|lang1 symbol=Ղ|lang2=[[Hebrew numerals|Hebrew]]|lang2 symbol=<span style="font-size:150%;">צ / ץ</span>|lang3=[[Babylonian cuneiform numerals|Babylonian numeral]]|lang3 symbol=𒐕𒌍|lang4=[[Egyptian numerals|Egyptian hieroglyph]]|lang4 symbol=<span style="font-size:200%;">𓎎</span>}}

In the English language, the numbers 90 and 19 are often confused, as they sound very similar. When carefully enunciated, they differ in which syllable is stressed: 19 /naɪnˈtiːn/ vs 90 /ˈnaɪnti/.

== In mathematics ==
90 is a [[pronic number]] as it is the [[Multiplication|product]] of [[9]] and [[10]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oeis.org/A002378|title=Sloane's A002378 : Oblong (or promic, pronic, or heteromecic) numbers|website=The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|publisher=OEIS Foundation|access-date=2016-05-29}}</ref> and along with [[12 (number)|12]] and [[56 (number)|56]], one of only a few pronic numbers whose digits in [[Base ten|decimal]] are also successive. 90 is divisible by the sum of its [[Decimal|base-ten]] digits, which makes it the thirty-second [[Harshad number]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oeis.org/A005349|title=Sloane's A005349 : Niven (or Harshad) numbers|website=The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|publisher=OEIS Foundation|access-date=2016-05-29}}</ref>

=== Properties of the number ===

*90 is the only number to have an aliquot sum of [[144 (number)|144]]&nbsp;=&nbsp;12<sup>2</sup>. 

*Only three numbers have a set of [[divisor]]s that generate a sum equal to 90: they are [[40 (number)|40]], [[58 (number)|58]], and [[89 (number)|89]].<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A000203 |...the sum of the divisors of n. |access-date=2023-06-30 }}</ref> 

*90 is also the twentieth [[abundant number|abundant]]<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A005101 |Abundant numbers (sum of divisors of m exceeds 2m). |access-date=2023-06-23 }}</ref> and [[highly abundant number|highly abundant]]<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A002093 |Highly abundant numbers |access-date=2023-06-23 }}</ref> number (with [[20 (number)|20]] the first [[primitive abundant number]] and [[70 (number)|70]] the second).<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A071395 |Primitive abundant numbers (abundant numbers all of whose proper divisors are deficient numbers). |access-date=2023-06-23 }}</ref>

*The number of [[divisor]]s of 90 is 12.<ref name="OEIS-A000005">{{Cite OEIS|A000005|d(n) (also called tau(n) or sigma_0(n)), the number of divisors of n.}}</ref> Other smaller numbers with this property are [[sixty|60]], [[seventy-two|72]] and [[eighty-four|84]]. These four and [[ninety-six|96]] are the five double-digit numbers with exactly 12 divisors.<ref name="OEIS-A067128">{{Cite OEIS|A067128|Ramanujan's largely composite numbers}}</ref>

*90 is the tenth and largest number to hold an [[Euler totient]] value of [[24 (number)|24]];<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A000010 |Euler totient function phi(n): count numbers less than or equal to n and prime to n. |access-date=2024-01-16 }}</ref> no number has a totient that is 90, which makes it the eleventh [[nontotient]] (with [[50 (number)|50]] the fifth).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oeis.org/A005277|title=Sloane's A005277 : Nontotients|website=The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|publisher=OEIS Foundation|access-date=2016-05-29}}</ref> 

The twelfth [[triangular number]] [[78 (number)|78]]<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A000217 |Triangular numbers|access-date=2022-11-01 }}</ref> is the only number to have an [[aliquot sum]] equal to 90, aside from the [[Square number|square]] of the twenty-fourth prime, [[89 (number)|89]]<sup>2</sup> (which is [[centered octagonal number|centered octagonal]]).<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A001065 |Sum of proper divisors (or aliquot parts) of n: sum of divisors of n that are less than n. |access-date=2023-06-30 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite OEIS |A016754 |Centered octagonal numbers. |access-date=2023-07-02 }}</ref> 90 is equal to the fifth sum of ''non-triangular'' numbers, respectively between the fifth and sixth triangular numbers, [[15 (number)|15]] and [[21 (number)|21]] (equivalently [[16 (number)|16]]&nbsp;+&nbsp;[[17 (number)|17]]&nbsp;...&nbsp;+&nbsp;[[20 (number)|20]]).<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A006002 |...also: Sum of the nontriangular numbers between successive triangular numbers. }}</ref> It is also twice [[45 (number)|45]], which is the ninth triangular number, and the second-smallest sum of twelve non-zero integers, from two through thirteen <math>\{2,3,...,13\}</math>.

90 can be expressed as the sum of distinct non-zero [[Square number|squares]] in six ways, more than any smaller number (see image):<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A033461 |Number of partitions of n into distinct squares. }}</ref>

<math>(9^{2}+3^{2}),(8^{2}+5^{2}+1^{2}),(7^{2}+5^{2}+4^{2}),(8^{2}+4^{2}+3^{2}+1^{2}),(7^{2}+6^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}),(6^{2}+5^{2}+4^{2}+3^{2}+2^{2})</math>.

[[File:square-sum-90.png|right|thumb|90 as the sum of distinct nonzero squares]]

The square of eleven 11<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;121 is the ninetieth indexed [[composite number]],<ref name="A02808">{{Cite OEIS |A02808 |The composite numbers. }}</ref> where the sum of integers <math>\{2,3,...,11\}</math> is [[65 (number)|65]], which in-turn represents the composite index of 90.<ref name="A02808" /> In the [[fractional part]] of the [[decimal expansion]] of the reciprocal of [[11 (number)|11]] in [[Decimal|base-10]], "90" repeats periodically (when leading zeroes are moved to the end).<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A060283 |Periodic part of decimal expansion of reciprocal of n-th prime (leading 0's moved to end). }}</ref>

The eighteenth [[Stirling number of the second kind]] <math>S(n,k)</math> is 90, from a <math>n</math> of 6 and a <math>k</math> of 3, as the number of ways of dividing a [[Set theory|set]] of six objects into three [[Empty set|non-empty subset]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oeis.org/A008277|title=Sloane's A008277 :Triangle of Stirling numbers of the second kind|website=The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|publisher=OEIS Foundation|access-date=2021-12-24}}</ref> 90 is also the sixteenth [[Perrin number]] from a sum of [[39 (number)|39]] and [[51 (number)|51]], whose difference is [[12 (number)|12]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oeis.org/A001608|title=Sloane's A001608 : Perrin sequence|website=The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|publisher=OEIS Foundation|access-date=2016-05-29}}</ref>

==== Prime sextuplets ====

The members of the first [[prime sextuplet]] ([[7]], [[11 (number)|11]], [[13 (number)|13]], 17, [[19 (number)|19]], [[23 (number)|23]]) generate a [[Addition|sum]] equal to 90, and the difference between respective members of the first and second prime sextuplets is also 90, where the second prime sextuplet is ([[97 (number)|97]], [[101 (number)|101]], [[103 (number)|103]], [[107 (number)|107]], [[109 (number)|109]], [[113 (number)|113]]).<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A022008 |Initial member of prime sextuples (p, p+4, p+6, p+10, p+12, p+16). |access-date=2023-06-11 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite OEIS |A200503 |Record (maximal) gaps between prime sextuplets (p, p+4, p+6, p+10, p+12, p+16). |access-date=2023-06-23 }}</ref> The last member of the second prime sextuplet, 113, is the 30th [[prime number]]. Since prime sextuplets are formed from prime members of lower order [[Prime k-tuple|prime ''k''-tuples]], 90 is also a record maximal gap between various smaller pairs of prime ''k''-tuples (which include [[Prime quadruplet#Prime quintuplets|quintuplets]], [[Prime quadruplet|quadruplets]], and [[Prime triplet|triplets]]).{{efn|1=90 is the record gap between the first pair of [[Prime quadruplet#Prime quintuplets|prime quintuplets]] of the form {{math|(''p'', ''p''+2, ''p''+6, ''p''+8, ''p''+12)}} ([[OEIS:A201073|A201073]]), while 90 is a record between the second and third prime quintuplets that have the form {{math|(''p'', ''p''+4, ''p''+6, ''p''+10, ''p''+12)}} ([[OEIS:A201062|A201062]]). Regarding [[prime quadruplet]]s, 90 is the gap record between the second and third set of quadruplets ([[OEIS:A113404|A113404]]). [[Prime triplet]]s of the form {{math|(''p'', ''p''+4, ''p''+6)}} have a third record maximal gap of 90 between the second and ninth triplets ([[OEIS:A201596|A201596]]), and while there is no record gap of 90 for prime triplets of the form {{math|(''p'', ''p''+2, ''p''+6)}}, the first and third record gaps are of [[6]] and 60 ([[OEIS:A201598|A201598]]), which are also ''unitary perfect numbers'' like 90 ([[OEIS:A002827|A002827]]). }}

==== Unitary perfect number ====

90 is the third [[unitary perfect number]] (after [[6]] and [[60 (number)|60]]), since it is the sum of its [[unitary divisor]]s excluding itself,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oeis.org/A002827|title=Sloane's A002827 : Unitary perfect numbers|website=The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|publisher=OEIS Foundation|access-date=2016-05-29}}</ref> and because it is equal to the sum of a subset of its divisors, it is also the twenty-first [[semiperfect number]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oeis.org/A005835|title=Sloane's A005835 : Pseudoperfect (or semiperfect) numbers|website=The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|publisher=OEIS Foundation|access-date=2016-05-29}}</ref>

=== Right angle ===

[[File:Right angle.svg|right|120px|thumb|A [[right angle]] measures ninety [[Degree (angle)|degrees]].]]

An angle measuring 90&nbsp;degrees is called a [[right angle]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Friedman |first=Erich |date=n.d. |title=What's Special About This Number? |url=http://www.stetson.edu/~efriedma/numbers.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180223062027/http://www.stetson.edu/~efriedma/numbers.html |archive-date=February 23, 2018 |access-date=February 27, 2023 |website=www.stetson.edu}}</ref> In normal [[space]], the [[interior angles]] of a [[rectangle]] measure 90&nbsp;[[Degree (angle)|degrees]] each, while in a [[right triangle]], the angle opposing the [[hypotenuse]] measures 90&nbsp;degrees, with the other two angles adding up to 90 for a total of {{num|180}}&nbsp;degrees.

=== Icosahedral symmetry ===

[[File:Witting polytope.png|205px|left|thumb|The [[Witting polytope]], with ninety [[Complex polytope#van Oss polygon|van Oss polytopes]]]]

==== Solids ====

The [[rhombic enneacontahedron]] is a [[zonohedron]] with a total of 90 [[Rhombus|rhombic]] [[Face (geometry)|faces]]: 60 broad rhombi akin to those in the [[rhombic dodecahedron]] with diagonals in <math>1:\sqrt2</math> ratio, and another 30 slim rhombi with diagonals in <math>1:\varphi^{2}</math> [[golden ratio]]. The obtuse angle of the broad rhombic faces is also the [[dihedral angle]] of a [[regular icosahedron]], with the [[obtuse angle]] in the faces of [[Golden rhombus|golden rhombi]] equal to the dihedral angle of a [[regular octahedron]] and the [[Tetrahedron#Angles and distances|tetrahedral vertex-center-vertex]] angle, which is also the angle between [[Plateau's laws|Plateau borders]]: 109.471°. It is the dual polyhedron to the [[rectified truncated icosahedron]], a [[near-miss Johnson solid]]. On&nbsp;the other hand, the [[final stellation of the icosahedron]] has 90 edges. It also has 92 vertices like the rhombic enneacontahedron, when interpreted as a [[simple polyhedron]]. Meanwhile, the [[truncated dodecahedron]] and [[truncated icosahedron]] both have 90 [[Edge (geometry)|edges]]. A further four uniform [[Uniform star polyhedron|star polyhedra]] ([[Truncated great dodecahedron|U<sub>37</sub>]], [[Truncated great icosahedron|U<sub>55</sub>]], [[Small stellated truncated dodecahedron|U<sub>58</sub>]], [[Great stellated truncated dodecahedron|U<sub>66</sub>]]) and four uniform [[Uniform polyhedron compound|compound polyhedra]] ([[Compound of ten triangular prisms|UC<sub>32</sub>]], [[Compound of six pentagonal prisms|UC<sub>34</sub>]], [[Compound of six pentagrammic prisms|UC<sub>36</sub>]], [[Compound of five truncated tetrahedra|UC<sub>55</sub>]]) contain 90 edges or [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]].

==== Witting polytope ====

The [[Dual polyhedron#Dual polytopes and tessellations|self-dual]] [[Witting polytope]] contains ninety [[Complex polytope#van Oss polygon|van Oss polytopes]] such that sections by the common [[Plane (geometry)|plane]] of two non-orthogonal [[hyperplane]]s of symmetry passing through the [[Center (geometry)#General polygons|center]] yield [[Complex polytope|complex]] <sub>3</sub>{4}<sub>3</sub> [[Möbius–Kantor polygon]]s.<ref name="Coxeter">{{Cite book |author=Coxeter |first=Harold Scott MacDonald |title=Regular Complex Polytopes |url=https://archive.org/details/regularcomplexpo0000coxe/page/132/mode/2up |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1974 |edition=1st |pages=133 |author-link=H. S. M. Coxeter |isbn=978-0-52-1201254 |url-access=registration }}</ref> The [[root vector]]s of [[Group of Lie type|simple Lie group]] [[E8 (mathematics)|'''E<sub>8</sub>''']] are represented by the [[Vertex (geometry)|vertex]] arrangement of the <math>4_{21}</math> [[4 21 polytope|polytope]], which shares [[240 (number)|240]] vertices with the Witting polytope in four-dimensional [[Complex coordinate space|complex space]]. By [[Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter|Coxeter]], the incidence matrix [[Configuration (polytope)|configuration]] of the Witting polytope can be represented as:

:<math>\left[\begin{smallmatrix}40&9&12\\4&90&4\\12&9&40\end{smallmatrix}\right]</math> or <math>\left[\begin{smallmatrix}40&12&12\\2&240&2\\12&12&40\end{smallmatrix}\right]</math>

This Witting configuration when reflected under the [[finite space]] <math>\operatorname{PG}{(3,2^{2})}</math> splits into 85&nbsp;=&nbsp;45&nbsp;+&nbsp;40 points ''and'' planes, alongside 27&nbsp;+&nbsp;90&nbsp;+&nbsp;240&nbsp;=&nbsp;357 lines.<ref name="Coxeter" />

Whereas the rhombic enneacontahedron is the [[Zonohedron#Zonohedrification|zonohedrification]] of the regular dodecahedron,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hart |first=George W. |author-link=George W. Hart |url=http://www.georgehart.com/virtual-polyhedra/zonohedrification.html |title=Zonohedrification |website=Virtual Polyhedra (The Encyclopedia of Polyhedra) |access-date=2023-06-23 }}</ref> a [[Witting polytope#The honeycomb of Witting polytopes|honeycomb]] of Witting polytopes holds vertices [[isomorphic]] to the E<sub>8</sub> [[E8 lattice|lattice]], whose symmetries can be traced back to the regular icosahedron via the [[Icosian|icosian ring]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Baez |first=John C. |author-link=John C. Baez |title=From the Icosahedron to E<sub>8</sub> |journal=London Math. Soc. Newsletter |volume=476 |pages=18–23 |publisher=[[London Mathematical Society]] |year=2018 |location=London, UK |bibcode=2017arXiv171206436B |arxiv=1712.06436 |mr=3792329 |s2cid=119151549 |zbl=1476.51020 }}</ref>

=== Cutting an annulus ===

The maximal number of pieces that can be obtained by cutting an [[Annulus (mathematics)|annulus]] with twelve cuts is 90 (and equivalently, the number of 12-dimensional [[polyomino]]es that are ''prime'').<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A000096 |a(n) equal to n*(n+3)/2. }}</ref>
